links.outcome: Human-AI team performance under simulated positive, neutral, negative interaction (automation bias) vs standalone
links.effect: Automation bias degraded multi-reader performance but improved single-reader; AI triage sensitivity could drop 5.6 points to ~73.1% (6.7 below baseline) under negative interaction, while positive interaction gave +3.4 points over baseline.
links.quote: In the negative interaction case, however, the potential downside is significant.

links.outcome: Effect of simulated automation bias (readers agreeing with incorrect AI) on system sensitivity/specificity
links.effect: Negative interaction in AI triage dropped sensitivity by 5.6 points to about 73.1% and specificity to 93.5%; single-reader negative interaction lowered sensitivity/specificity to ~62.6% and 93.9%.
links.quote: The sensitivity can quickly drop by 5.6 percentage points to about 73.1% (6.7 percentage points lower than the baseline standard of care) and the specificity can drop to 93.5% when human readers follow the mistakes made by the AI reader.

links.outcome: AI reader and AI-integrated pathways compared with radiologists and standard of care on same data
links.effect: AI standalone sensitivity 75.0 vs 66.3% for mean individual radiologist; reader-replacement achieved 82.3% sensitivity and 96.3% specificity vs standard of care 79.8%/96.0%.
links.quote: The AI reader-replacement scenario produced higher system sensitivity (82.3%; 95% CI 81.5–83.1, P < 0.0025) and higher specificity (96.3%; 95% CI 96.2–96.3, P < 4.3 × 10 −6 ) than the current standard of care system (Fig. 3 A and Supplementary Table 2 ).

links.outcome: Performance of AI band-pass pathway where AI makes final decisions without human read
links.effect: AI band-pass without human reads for high/low scores gave 81.7% sensitivity, 96.6% specificity vs 79.8%/96.0% standard, with 80.7% fewer human reads; authors note lack of human decision-maker faces adoption challenges.
links.quote: However, having an AI reader make the final reading decision, without human involvement, faces challenges before clinical adoption.

links.outcome: Sequestered test set with separate development set for operating points, representative cohort
links.effect: Operating points were set on a separate development set (49,796 episodes); test set 149,105 episodes from representative screening years; external datasets benchmarked.
links.quote: All operating points were set on the development set (Supplementary Fig. 13 ).

links.effect: AI band-pass: sensitivity 81.7% vs 79.8%, specificity 96.6% vs 96.0%; 779 fewer false positives, 25 more cancers, −80.7% human reads.
links.quote: The AI band-pass screening scenario also achieved both higher system sensitivity (81.7%, P < 0.0058) and specificity (96.6%, P < 2.2 × 10 −25 ) than the current standard of care system (Fig. 3 A and Supplementary Table 2 ).

links.effect: AI standalone sensitivity was lower than standard care, 75.0% vs 79.8%; specificity was non-inferior, 96.0% vs 96.0%.
links.quote: However, operating as a sole reader, the AI reader had lower sensitivity (75.0 vs. 79.8%; P < 1.98 × 10 −5 ) at non-inferior specificity (96.0 vs. 96.0%: P = 0.56) than the current standard of care (two readers with arbitration; Supplementary Tables 1 , 2 ).

links.effect: Automation bias degraded multi-reader settings but improved single-reader; AI reader-replacement sensitivity fell below standard care only after roughly 30%+ discordant reversals.
links.quote: Automation bias degrades performance in multi-reader settings but improves it for single-readers.

links.effect: Band-pass did not require human reads for all cases yet had 779 fewer unnecessary recalls, 25 more cancers, and −80.7% human reads.
